stem: What are the two failure modes behind almost every tracheostomy emergency?
correct_choice: Obstruction and displacement
distractors: Infection and bleeding | Cuff rupture and stoma infection | Aspiration and pneumothorax

stem: Why is the inner cannula removed before a suction catheter is passed, rather than suctioning through it?
correct_choice: Removing it often clears the plug instantly and confirms true patency
distractors: It reduces the risk of infection | It is required before any oxygen can be given | It lets the cuff be deflated safely

stem: If a suction catheter passes freely well beyond the tip of the tracheostomy tube, what has this confirmed?
correct_choice: The tube is patent
distractors: The patient no longer needs oxygen | The cuff is properly inflated | The tract is mature

stem: A nurse pushes a popped-out fresh trach back in and it slides in with no resistance at all — does this prove correct placement?
correct_choice: No — a false passage can accept the tube just as easily
distractors: Yes, resistance-free insertion always means correct placement | Yes, but only in patients over 65 | No, but only if the patient is coughing

stem: Beyond simply 'not working,' why is forcing a dislodged fresh trach back into a false passage actively dangerous rather than just ineffective?
correct_choice: It can cause surgical emphysema and gives false reassurance that delays the real fix
distractors: It always causes immediate cardiac arrest | It permanently destroys the tracheostomy stoma | It has no additional danger beyond simple obstruction

stem: Why does the NTSP Red algorithm never direct initial oxygenation effort at the face, not even briefly, for a laryngectomy patient?
correct_choice: It delivers no oxygen and wastes critical time
distractors: It can trigger a vasovagal response | It dries out the laryngectomy stoma | It is only skipped in pediatric laryngectomy patients

stem: Why does a delayed recognition of displacement tend to be more immediately lethal, minute-for-minute, than a delayed recognition of obstruction?
correct_choice: Displacement can cause abrupt total loss of ventilation with little warning, unlike gradual obstruction
distractors: Obstruction is always more lethal than displacement | Displacement only occurs in patients already on a ventilator | Both carry identical time pressure in every case

stem: Before placing a speaking valve on a tracheostomy patient, what is the one absolute prerequisite regarding the cuff?
correct_choice: Cuff fully deflated
distractors: Cuff inflated to 20 cmH2O | Cuff partially deflated | Cuff status doesn't matter for valve use

stem: Walk through the exact physiological sequence that makes a speaking valve dangerous if the cuff is left inflated.
correct_choice: Air keeps entering but cannot exit, causing breath stacking
distractors: The cuff pops and the tube falls out | The valve fails to open on inhalation | Oxygen delivery through the valve is blocked

stem: True or false: a standard tracheostomy speaking valve can be used on a total laryngectomy patient.
correct_choice: False — there is no upper airway exit for exhaled air
distractors: True — it works the same as in a tracheostomy patient | True — but only if the cuff is inflated | False — but only because it isn't tolerated well

stem: hard
correct_choice: Why is it unsafe to inflate a tracheostomy cuff to 'the usual 5 mL' by habit, without checking pressure?
distractors: Volume-to-pressure varies by tube and trachea, so a fixed volume is unreliable
column11: 5 mL is always too little for any adult trachea | Syringe inflation cannot reach therapeutic pressure | Cuffs lose air only through the pilot balloon, not the trachea

stem: A patient's heart rate drops sharply while the suction catheter is still in the airway. What do you do immediately?
correct_choice: Stop suctioning and withdraw the catheter immediately
distractors: Continue suctioning to finish clearing secretions faster | Increase suction pressure to clear secretions quicker | Reposition the patient before withdrawing the catheter

stem: What does it mean to call a tracheostomy patient a "partial neck breather"?
correct_choice: Upper airway still connects to the lungs
distractors: Upper airway is permanently sealed off | They breathe only through the mouth | They have no tracheostomy tube in place

stem: A tracheostomy (partial neck breather) patient desaturates. Which route(s) can you use to give oxygen?
correct_choice: Face and stoma, either or both
distractors: Stoma only, never the face | Face only, never the stoma | Neither — bag immediately instead

concept: Unsure trach vs laryngectomy — safest act
stem: You are unsure whether a crashing neck-airway patient is a tracheostomy or a laryngectomy. What is the single safest immediate action for oxygen delivery?
correct_choice: Apply oxygen to both the face and the stoma
distractors: Apply oxygen to the face only until confirmed | Apply oxygen to the stoma only until confirmed | Withhold oxygen until the chart is checked

stem: In one anatomical sentence, why does oxygen applied to the face do nothing for a total laryngectomy patient?
correct_choice: No anatomical path from mouth/nose to the lungs exists
distractors: The oxygen concentration is too low at the face | Laryngectomy patients cannot tolerate nasal cannulas | Their lungs no longer require external oxygen

stem: An expanding neck hematoma is threatening the airway. Name the three things the bedside RN should be doing at once.
correct_choice: Call for help, bring airway cart, prep bedside wound opening
distractors: Call for help, order a CT, and wait | Reassure the patient and recheck vitals in 30 minutes | Apply ice and elevate the head of bed only

stem: You notice a tracheostomy tube pulsating with the heartbeat. What must you suspect?
correct_choice: Tracheo-innominate artery fistula
distractors: Normal tube movement with breathing | A sign the cuff needs more air | A sign of tube displacement only

stem: Why does a sentinel bleed in a radiated, previously operated neck raise concern specifically for carotid blowout?
correct_choice: Radiation-damaged vessel wall is starting to fail
distractors: Sentinel bleeds are unrelated to vessel integrity | It indicates a new, unrelated wound infection | It only matters if the patient is anticoagulated

stem: On free flap checks, a dusky, blue, congested appearance points to which type of vascular compromise?
correct_choice: Venous compromise
distractors: Arterial compromise | Normal healing flap | Lymphedema

stem: You palpate crackling under the skin around a fresh tracheostomy site. What is this finding called?
correct_choice: Subcutaneous emphysema
distractors: Normal post-op swelling | Wound infection | An expected finding requiring no action

stem: What is one of the earliest bedside signs that a trach patient's secretions are becoming dangerously thick?
correct_choice: Secretions become thick, tenacious, or crusty
distractors: Secretions become thinner and more watery | The patient's voice suddenly improves | The stoma dressing stays perfectly dry

stem: Beyond routine hygiene, what specific airway risk does a scheduled inner cannula check catch that waiting for symptoms would miss?
correct_choice: It catches partial occlusion before it becomes a full obstruction
distractors: It confirms the outer cannula size is still correct | It verifies the patient's swallow function | It checks whether the cuff pressure is in range

stem: Why can a trach patient aspirate SILENTLY even with the cuff inflated, with no coughing or choking to alert the nurse?
correct_choice: The trach blunts laryngeal sensation and the protective cough reflex
distractors: The cuff physically blocks all aspirated material from being felt | Silent aspiration is a myth in tracheostomy patients | It only happens when the cuff is fully deflated

stem: A trach patient is being sent to CT for a 20-minute scan. Why must the full bedside emergency kit go with them, not just a portable oxygen tank?
correct_choice: Airway emergencies can happen in transit, where bedside equipment can't reach
distractors: CT scanners already contain trach emergency equipment | It is only required for laryngectomy patients, not trach patients | Portable oxygen alone fully covers any airway emergency

stem: Which of the two failure modes — obstruction or displacement — is the more common cause of tracheostomy emergencies on a general floor?
correct_choice: Obstruction (mucus plug)
distractors: Displacement | They are exactly equal in frequency | Neither — infection is most common

stem: Why must the speaking valve or cap come off BEFORE anything else in a distressed trach patient, rather than going straight to suctioning?
correct_choice: A one-way valve traps air in if the patient can't exhale
distractors: It makes suctioning more comfortable | It has to be cleaned between uses | It interferes with the pulse oximeter

stem: You've removed the valve and inner cannula and passed a catheter with no obstruction found, but the chest still doesn't move with bagging via the tube. What should you now suspect?
correct_choice: Displacement or a false passage
distractors: A simple mucus plug further down | Cuff over-inflation | Normal post-suction coughing

stem: Can a dislodged fresh (under 5–7 day old) tracheostomy tube be safely pushed back in blindly at the bedside?
correct_choice: No, never attempt blind reinsertion
distractors: Yes, if done within one minute | Yes, if the patient is calm | Only if the RN has done it before

stem: During bag-valve ventilation through a suspected malpositioned tube, what physical exam finding on the neck should immediately raise suspicion for a false passage?
correct_choice: Crepitus / subcutaneous emphysema around the neck
distractors: Bilateral wheeze on auscultation | Jugular venous distension only | Warm, dry skin at the stoma

stem: A 'tubed' laryngectomy patient's small stoma tube falls out. Is the rescue response the same as for a displaced tracheostomy — occlude the stoma and ventilate at the face?
correct_choice: No — ventilate directly at the stoma; face ventilation is useless
distractors: Yes — the response is identical for both populations | Yes, but only if the patient is hemodynamically stable | No — laryngectomy patients cannot be bag-mask ventilated at all

stem: How do suction catheter behavior and capnography together help you tell obstruction from displacement when the presentation looks similar?
correct_choice: Catheter resistance suggests obstruction; a missing CO2 waveform despite bagging suggests displacement
distractors: Catheter resistance always means displacement | Capnography cannot distinguish the two situations | A waveform confirms obstruction, not displacement

stem: A patient's cuff was confirmed deflated for a valve trial this morning. That afternoon a different nurse wants to reapply the same valve. What must happen first?
correct_choice: Reconfirm cuff deflation right before this application
distractors: Trust the morning documentation | Ask the patient if they feel short of breath first | Only recheck if the patient looks distressed

stem: The cuff syringe shows only 2 mL still in the pilot balloon — 'basically down.' Is it safe to place the speaking valve?
correct_choice: No — it must be fully deflated, not partially
distractors: Yes — a few mL of residual air is negligible | Yes, as long as pressure reads under 20 cmH2O | It only matters if the patient reports discomfort

stem: Anatomically, why exactly does a one-way speaking valve have no safe exit for exhaled air after a total laryngectomy?
correct_choice: The trachea is a blind-ending stoma with no route to the upper airway
distractors: The vocal cords are removed but the trachea still connects to the pharynx | The cuff cannot be deflated after laryngectomy | The stoma is too small for exhaled air to pass

stem: easy
correct_choice: What device should be used to accurately measure and set tracheostomy cuff pressure?
distractors: A cuff pressure manometer
column11: A pulse oximeter | A 10 mL syringe alone | A stethoscope over the trachea

stem: Explain the mechanism by which suctioning can cause sudden bradycardia.
correct_choice: Catheter stimulation of vagal nerve endings triggers a reflex slowdown
distractors: Suction pressure directly compresses the carotid artery | Hypoxia alone always causes bradycardia within seconds | The cuff pushes on the vagus nerve during suctioning

stem: What does it mean to call a total laryngectomy patient a "total neck breather"?
correct_choice: 100% of breathing occurs through the stoma
distractors: They still breathe partly through the nose | Their trach tube can be removed at will | Their mouth is their main airway

stem: A total laryngectomy patient desaturates. Which route MUST you use to deliver oxygen?
correct_choice: Stoma only
distractors: Face mask only | Nasal cannula only | Either face or stoma

concept: Unsure trach vs laryngectomy — safest act
stem: Before touching any neck-airway patient, what is the single question you must answer first?
correct_choice: Is this patient a tracheostomy or a laryngectomy?
distractors: What size is the trach tube? | When was the tube last changed? | Is the cuff currently inflated?

stem: During resuscitation of a laryngectomy patient, where do you seal the bag-mask to ventilate them?
correct_choice: Over the stoma
distractors: Over the mouth and nose | Over the mouth only, nose occluded | Split — half the breaths to each route

stem: A post-op neck patient feels their neck getting tight and their voice change. What complication must you suspect immediately?
correct_choice: Expanding neck hematoma
distractors: Normal post-op swelling | Anxiety attack | Allergic reaction

stem: A tracheo-innominate fistula is suspected and actively bleeding. What is the FIRST temporizing maneuver at the bedside?
correct_choice: Hyperinflate the tracheostomy cuff
distractors: Deflate the cuff to relieve pressure | Remove the tube entirely and pack the stoma | Give antifibrinolytic medication IV first

stem: In a radiated neck, a small wound bleed stops on its own. Is this reassuring?
correct_choice: No — it is a sentinel bleed warning sign
distractors: Yes — stopped bleeding means it resolved | Only concerning if it happens twice | Only concerning if the patient is hypotensive

stem: On free flap checks, a pale, cool flap with no Doppler signal points to which type of vascular compromise?
correct_choice: Arterial compromise
distractors: Venous compromise | Expected flap edema | Dehydration

stem: Why is new or worsening subcutaneous emphysema after a tracheostomy a red flag rather than a benign finding?
correct_choice: It can signal tracheal injury or an accompanying pneumothorax
distractors: It always resolves spontaneously and needs no monitoring | It only ever indicates cuff over-inflation | It confirms tube displacement into the esophagus

stem: A trach patient on a passive HME has secretions that are already thick and increasingly hard to clear despite the HME being in place. What is the correct next humidification step, and why?
correct_choice: Switch to active heated humidification — the HME can't add extra moisture
distractors: Increase suction frequency and leave the HME in place | Add a second HME in series for double filtration | Switch to a smaller inner cannula to widen the lumen

stem: Why can pulse oximetry stay reassuringly normal even as a mucus plug is silently developing overnight?
correct_choice: SpO2 only drops once narrowing is severe, lagging behind the true process
distractors: SpO2 always falls immediately with any secretion buildup | Pulse oximeters cannot function on trach patients | SpO2 rises falsely high when secretions thicken

stem: Why must a new trach patient have a formal swallow evaluation before starting an oral diet, rather than a nurse simply judging by cuff status alone?
correct_choice: Because aspiration can be silent and needs formal mechanical assessment
distractors: Because diet orders legally require a dietitian consult only | Because cuff status alone always predicts swallow safety | Because trach patients are never allowed oral intake

stem: What two spare tracheostomy tubes must be kept at every trach patient's bedside?
correct_choice: Same size AND one size smaller
distractors: Same size and one size larger | Only the same size, doubled up | Any size, as long as one is present
